answer_text:
Assume \(a<b\). For any integrable \(f\),

\[
\left|\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\right|\le \int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt.
\]

Suppose a constant \(C>0\) worked for every integrable \(f\). Let

\[
f(t)=
\begin{cases}
1, & a\le t\le \frac{a+b}{2},\\
-1, & \frac{a+b}{2}<t\le b.
\end{cases}
\]

Then \(f\) is integrable,

\[
\int_a^b f(t)\,dt=0,
\qquad
\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt=b-a>0.
\]

Plugging into the proposed inequality gives

\[
0 \ge C(b-a),
\]

which is impossible if \(C>0\). Hence no positive constant \(C\) can work for all integrable functions.

If \(C\le 0\), then \(\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt\ge 0\), so

\[
C\int_a^b |f(t)|\,dt\le 0\le \left|\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\right|,
\]

so the inequality holds trivially.

\[
\boxed{\text{No positive constant } C \text{ exists; the only universal constants are } C\le 0.}
\]
